viewport.why: 360 by 780 of CSS at four times scale: a 1440 by 3120 Android, which is a phone somebody owns. The stills were shot at 480 by 1040 at three times scale — the same 1440 by 3120 the brief asks for, but laid out at a logical width no phone has and 120 points wider than every clip in the set. A coherence critic found what that hid: two Us rows that read fully at 480 truncate to 'the second one · the…' and 'tape the gap in the bac…' at the clip's width, and the calendar glance wraps into a line the card cuts. Same pixels, same minimum, same layout width as the clips and as the phone.

steps.why: So the row that is taken back is the newest one rather than the last thing noor said in the seeded year. The twelfth capture proved the difference: the daemon really withdrew a message — its log says `took back 01M1M59VY0YA13H9M86HTA6XNP` — and the still framed the end of the thread, where the three rows that fit are the staged states, with the withdrawal months above them. A chat at 360 by 780 has a 372 point viewport and holds three rows; a mark that is not next to the others cannot be in the same picture as them.

Noor takes back the last thing she sent. `taken_back` was empty and `message_delete` zero in every region report in the set, so the scrollTo below was asking to frame a mark that was nowhere in the data — a messenger critic counted taking a note back as one of two capabilities this artifact enumerates and no artifact shows. The withdrawal happens on the far phone, so what the near phone draws is a note that was really taken away from it.

Framed on the three marks rather than pinned to the end. A messenger critic measured two of the eleven capabilities this artifact is supposed to enumerate — editing and taking a message back — visible in no artifact at all: the report named an edited row and the still's first drawn sheet began 84 px below where that row ended, so it was just off the top. `end` frames the newest note and the staging writes four more rows after the edit. This asks for the tightest stretch that holds an edited row, a row taken back and one still in the outbox, and the framing machinery measures what actually lands on the glass and keeps the best it finds.
